## HOW THE EXTRACTION PROTECTS ITSELF -- V-2

Gate 25's first version stripped `<b>GatewayGuard</b> Checkup` into a **double
space**, so a two-word match missed it and the Checkup name rule was
undercounted **19 -> 3**. Every matcher here is run first against a control it
**must** match, and the script **exits 2 and writes nothing** if any control
fails. **15 controls passed on this run** -- that number is counted by the
script, not typed, because a hardcoded one goes stale the moment a control is
added.

**The controls caught a live defect in gate 25 on their first run.** The
switch-as-verb pattern published in the 2026-08-12 report and used by
`Run-CopyCheck.bat` is:

```
\bswitch(es|ed|ing)?\s+(it|them|this|that|the\s+\w+\s+)?(on|off)\b
```

The object alternatives `it|them|this|that` carry **no trailing `\s+`**, while
the `the\s+\w+\s+` branch does. So it matches *"switch off"* and *"switch the
firewall on"*, and **cannot match "switch it off"** -- the commonest form of
the banned verb, and the exact phrasing the rule itself quotes as its example
(*"It can switch it off with your permission"*). The pattern here is corrected;
**`Tool\Check-Copy-2026-08-13.ps1` still carries the original and should be
fixed before gate 25 is trusted on this word.** This is the same class as the
3-versus-5 undercount: an absence produced by the matcher.

The whitespace collapse that repairs the fusion has exactly one failure mode:
intra-word markup like `Gateway<b>Guard</b>`, which would become two words.
That case is **detected, not assumed away**.

**Intra-word markup found:** **None.** No intra-word markup on any page, so the whitespace collapse could not have split a word.

Advertising ID

Setting 11 of 19

### Advertising ID

Windows assigns your PC a unique tracking number that apps use to follow your activity and show you targeted ads. Turning it off removes that number and stops apps from tracking you across different programs.

▶ Your decision

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your Advertising ID setting, which lets apps show you personalized ads. It can turn that off with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup turned off the Advertising ID with your approval. You can turn it back on at any time — the steps are below.

#### Why you might want this off

The Advertising ID is a tracking number Microsoft assigns to your PC. Apps that use it can see what you do across different programs and use that information to target you with ads. Think of it like a loyalty card number — except you did not sign up for it, and the data goes to advertisers you have never heard of.

Turning it off does not stop you from seeing ads. It just means the ads you see are not based on tracking what you do on your own PC. This is more than a taste: a record of what you do, built on your own machine and handed to advertisers you have never heard of, stops getting longer the moment you turn it off.

#### How to turn it off

Press the Windows key , type Privacy settings , and press Enter .

In the left sidebar, click General .

Find Let apps show me personalized ads by using my advertising ID . The toggle should be Off . If it is On, click it to turn it Off.

#### How to turn it back on if you want it

Press the Windows key , type Privacy settings , press Enter .

Click General in the left sidebar.

Toggle Let apps show me personalized ads by using my advertising ID to On .

#### What to expect

With the Advertising ID off, apps can no longer track your activity across programs to serve targeted ads. Your PC works exactly the same in every other way. No restart is needed. If you use apps from the Microsoft Store, you may notice ads become less targeted over time — that is the expected result.

This is more than a taste. The tracking number lets apps build a record of what you do across programs and hand it to advertisers. Checkup turns it off with your permission, and you can turn it back on whenever you like.

Home ›
Guide ›
BitLocker Data Encryption

Setting 8 of 19

### BitLocker Data Encryption

BitLocker scrambles everything on your hard drive so it’s unreadable without your password. If your laptop is lost or stolen, the thief cannot read your files — even if they remove the drive and plug it into another PC.

✓ Checkup walks you through this

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your drive’s encryption. On Windows 11 Home this is called Device Encryption; on Windows 11 Pro it is called BitLocker. Checkup never starts encryption without your explicit permission.

Action taken: Checkup walked you through enabling encryption and saving your recovery key to at least two safe locations, with your approval at each step. This is one of the few settings where Checkup guides you step by step rather than applying the change automatically — because the recovery key is critical and must be saved before encryption begins.

#### Why this matters

If your laptop is ever stolen, encryption is what protects your files. Without it, anyone with physical access to your drive can read everything on it — your documents, photos, passwords saved in your browser, everything — in minutes, using free tools.

With encryption on, the data on the drive is scrambled. Without your password (or your recovery key), it’s unreadable. The laptop can be wiped and resold. Your data stays private.

#### How to check it yourself

On Windows 11 Home : Open Settings > Privacy & security > Device encryption . If the toggle says On , your drive is encrypted.

On Windows 11 Pro : Open Settings > Privacy & security > Device security > BitLocker drive encryption . It should say BitLocker on next to your C: drive.

To check from the Start menu on either edition: press the Windows key and search for BitLocker . Open Manage BitLocker . The C: drive should show BitLocker on or On .

#### Your recovery key — do not skip this

Save your recovery key before encryption is complete. The recovery key is a 48-digit number that lets you access your drive if you ever forget your password or if Windows asks for it during startup. If you lose the key and forget your password, your files cannot be recovered — not by Microsoft, not by GatewayGuard, not by anyone.

Save your recovery key in at least two of these places:

Your Microsoft account online — go to account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey . If you signed into Windows with a Microsoft account, the key may already be saved here automatically.

A USB drive — save the key file to a USB drive you store somewhere safe (not with the laptop).

Printed on paper — print it and store it somewhere secure, like with important documents.

A password manager — if you use one, paste the key as a secure note.

GatewayGuard showed you this key during setup. If you saved it then, you’re done. If you cannot remember saving it, check your Microsoft account at the link above before doing anything else.

#### What to expect

Encryption runs in the background and does not slow down your PC during normal use. The initial encryption process (the first time you turn it on) may take 30 minutes to a few hours depending on how much is on your drive — you can use your PC normally while it runs.

Defender Real-Time Protection

Setting 2 of 19

### Defender Real-Time Protection

Microsoft Defender came with Microsoft Windows when you obtained Windows 11 Home or Pro. Real-time protection is the part that watches files and programs as you use them and blocks threats before they can run.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews Defender’s real-time protection, and which antivirus is primary on your PC. It can turn real-time protection back on with your permission.

Action taken: If real-time protection was off and no other antivirus had taken its place, Checkup flagged it and offered to turn it back on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

Your PC is protected from the moment you turn it on — but only if Defender is running. Real-time protection scans every file you open, every download, and every program you run. Without it, malware can install itself before anything notices.

Defender is free, built-in, and consistently rated by independent labs as one of the best antivirus engines available. You don’t need to pay for a separate product — you just need to make sure Defender is on and set up correctly.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key and type Windows Security , then press Enter .

Click Virus & threat protection .

Under Virus & threat protection settings , click Manage settings .

Confirm Real-time protection is set to On . The toggle should be blue.

Also check: Cloud-delivered protection — On. Automatic sample submission — On. These two help Defender identify new threats faster.

#### How to change it yourself

Open Windows Security (search from the Start menu).

Click Virus & threat protection , then Manage settings .

Click the toggle next to Real-time protection to turn it On.

If the toggle is grayed out and you can’t click it, another antivirus program is controlling this setting. You’ll see a message telling you which one. If you don’t recognize it or no longer use it, uninstall it first, then check Defender again.

#### What to expect

No restart required. Defender starts protecting your PC immediately once real-time protection is on.

Have Malwarebytes installed? If you’re using Malwarebytes Free as a companion scanner alongside Defender, that’s the recommended setup. Defender handles real-time protection; Malwarebytes runs manual scans as a second opinion. Both can run together without conflict.

Home ›

Diagnostic Data

Setting 12 of 19

### Diagnostic Data

Windows sends information about how your PC is running back to Microsoft. There are two levels: the minimum needed to keep Windows working, and a broader set that includes information about what you do on your PC. Checkup recommends the minimum.

▶ Your decision

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews how much diagnostic data your PC sends to Microsoft. It can limit this to the required minimum with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup set Diagnostic data to Required diagnostic data with your approval. This is the minimum level Windows needs to function and receive updates. It does not affect performance or updates in any way.

#### Why you might want the minimum

The optional level sends information about what you do on your PC. This includes which apps you use, how long you use them, which features you click on, and details about your browsing. Microsoft uses this to improve Windows — but it is your PC and your data, and you may not want to share it.

The required level sends only what Windows needs to work: basic device information, error reports, and update-related data. Your PC gets the same updates either way. The difference is how much information Microsoft receives about your daily use.

#### How to set it to the minimum

Press the Windows key , type Diagnostics & feedback , and press Enter .

Under Diagnostic data , you will see two options: Required diagnostic data and Optional diagnostic data .

Select Required diagnostic data . It should already be selected if Checkup ran successfully. If it shows Optional, click Required to change it.

#### What to expect

No restart required. Windows continues to receive all updates and works exactly the same. The change is that Microsoft receives less information about how you use your PC.

This is more than a taste. Nobody is reading your day — but a record of what you did on your own computer is kept where you cannot see it, for as long as someone decides to keep it, and you were never asked. Turning it down does not erase what is already there; it stops the list getting longer. Checkup makes this change with your permission.

Home ›

Edge Startup Boost

Setting 13 of 19

### Edge Startup Boost

Edge Startup Boost keeps parts of the Microsoft Edge browser running in the background so it opens faster when you click it. The trade-off: Edge is using memory and CPU even when you are not using it.

▶ Your decision

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews Edge Startup Boost and background running. It can turn them off with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup turned off Edge Startup Boost and background running with your approval. This is a convenience setting — if you prefer Edge to open as fast as possible and do not mind it running in the background, you can turn it back on at any time.

#### Why you might want this off

Edge runs in the background even when you are not using it. With Startup Boost on, Edge loads itself into memory when Windows starts so it is ready to go the moment you click it. That sounds helpful, but it means Edge is consuming RAM and running background processes you did not ask for.

On a PC with 8GB of RAM, this matters more. Every background process that runs when you are not using it is memory and CPU that is not available for what you are actually doing. Turning it off does not break Edge — it just opens a second or two slower.

#### How to check it yourself

Open Microsoft Edge .

Click the three dots ( ⋯ ) in the top right corner, then click Settings .

In the left sidebar, click System and performance .

Check two toggles: Startup boost and Continue running background extensions and apps when Microsoft Edge is closed . Both should be Off if you accepted Checkup’s recommendation.

#### How to change it back if you want

Open Edge › Settings › System and performance.

Toggle Startup boost to On .

Toggle Continue running background extensions and apps when Microsoft Edge is closed to On .

Note about pinned tabs: If you have tabs pinned in Edge, turning off background running means those pinned tabs will not refresh in the background while Edge is closed. They will reload when you open Edge next time.

#### What to expect

With Startup Boost off, Edge takes a second or two longer to open from a cold start. Once open, Edge works exactly the same as before. You may notice your PC starts up slightly faster and uses less memory overall.

Home ›
Guide ›
Fast Startup

Setting 18 of 19

### Fast Startup

Fast Startup makes your PC appear to shut down but actually saves your system state to disk so it can start up faster next time. The trade-off is that your PC never gets a true fresh start — and some Windows updates only finish installing after a proper restart.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your Fast Startup setting in Windows power options. It can turn it off with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup turned off Fast Startup with your approval. Your PC now does a proper full shutdown when you click Shut down. Startup will be a few seconds slower, but updates install completely and your PC starts in a fully clean state every time.

#### Why this matters

Fast Startup is not a real shutdown. When you click Shut down with Fast Startup on, Windows saves a snapshot of itself to your hard drive instead of closing everything down properly. The next time you start your PC, it loads that snapshot instead of starting fresh. This is faster, but it means your PC never truly resets between sessions.

The security concern is that some Windows updates require a proper full restart to finish installing. With Fast Startup on, a shutdown does not count — only a Restart does. This can leave your PC sitting with a partially installed security update without you realising it. Turning Fast Startup off means every shutdown is a proper one, and every startup is a fresh start.

#### How to turn it off

Press the Windows key , type Control Panel , and press Enter .

Click Hardware and Sound , then click Power Options .

In the left sidebar, click Choose what the power buttons do .

Click Change settings that are currently unavailable . This unlocks the checkboxes below.

Under Shutdown settings , find Turn on fast startup (recommended) . Remove the checkmark from this box.

Click Save changes .

Can not find the option? If Turn on fast startup is missing from the list, hibernation may be disabled on your PC. That is fine — Fast Startup requires hibernation to work, so if hibernation is off, Fast Startup is already off. No action needed.

#### How to check if it is already off

Open Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do .

Click Change settings that are currently unavailable .

Under Shutdown settings , check the Turn on fast startup box. It should have no checkmark. If it has a checkmark, remove it and save.

#### What to expect

Your PC will take a few seconds longer to start up — typically 10 to 30 seconds on a modern SSD, a bit more on an older hard drive. In exchange, every startup is a completely fresh start, and every Windows update finishes installing properly when you shut down. Your scheduled monthly and quarterly scan reminders still run. The reminders Checkup recommends setting up are scheduled inside Windows Task Scheduler and are not affected by this change.

Home ›

Firewall & Network Protection

Setting 7 of 19

### Firewall & Network Protection

The Windows Firewall monitors traffic coming into and going out of your PC over the network. When it’s on, it blocks uninvited connections — programs trying to reach your PC that you didn’t ask for.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews the Windows Firewall across all three network profiles: Domain, Private, and Public. It can turn on any profile that is off, with your permission.

Action taken: If any profile was off, Checkup flagged it and offered to turn it on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

The firewall is the gatekeeper for your network connection. Without it, other devices on your network — or programs already on your PC — can send and receive data without any filtering. On a home network that’s usually low-risk. On a public Wi-Fi network at a coffee shop or library, it matters a lot more.

Windows has three firewall profiles because your PC behaves differently depending on where it connects. All three should be on.

#### How to check it yourself

Open Windows Security and click Firewall & network protection .

You’ll see three entries: Domain network , Private network , and Public network .

Click each one and confirm the firewall toggle is set to On .

The active network (the one your PC is currently connected to) will be labeled (active) . That is the one to check right now.

#### How to change it yourself

Click the profile that is off (Domain, Private, or Public).

Click the toggle to turn the firewall On .

Repeat for any other profiles that are off.

No restart required.

#### What to expect

No restart required. The firewall is active immediately for new connections. Programs that were already running are not affected.

The firewall is separate from your antivirus. Defender handles malware scanning; the firewall handles network traffic. Both should be on at the same time — they protect against different things.

### Readable text

Home ›
Guide ›
Memory Integrity

Setting 16 of 19

### Memory Integrity (explained fully below)

There is one part of Windows that controls everything else on your PC. Memory Integrity keeps that part in a locked file location where other programs cannot reach it. Windows calls this setting Core isolation .

✓ Checkup can turn this on for you

#### What GatewayGuard Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your Memory Integrity setting. It can turn it on with your permission. A restart is required afterwards.

Action taken: If it was off and your PC can support it, Checkup asked for your approval and turned it on. Memory Integrity does not start working until you restart your PC.

#### Why this matters

One part of Windows controls everything else. Every program you run sits on top of it. If malware reaches that part, it is running underneath your antivirus — which makes it very hard to find and very hard to remove.

Memory Integrity puts that part in a locked file location. Other programs cannot get into it, so malware cannot get into it either.

This closes one of the last remaining ways for an attacker to take over a Windows PC completely. It is worth having on.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key and type Windows Security , then open it.

Click Device security in the list on the left.

Under Core isolation , click Core isolation details .

Look at the Memory integrity setting, then restart your PC when Windows asks.

Here is the full path. Use the Copy button if you would rather paste it than type it:

Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation details > Memory integrity
Copy

#### When to turn it on yourself

Turn it on yourself in any of these cases:

You checked using the steps above and it says Off .

GatewayGuard could not turn it on because it was not run as an administrator.

It was blocked by a driver before, and you have since updated that driver. See the next section.

You do not need to run Checkup again to do this. The four steps above are all it takes.

#### If Windows says a driver is blocking it

Leave it Off — forcing it can stop your PC from starting. Windows will name the driver that is blocking it. This is not a fault in your PC. It means one program on it uses an out-of-date driver, and that driver has not been updated to work with Memory Integrity yet.

A driver is the small program that lets Windows talk to a piece of your hardware — your printer, your screen, your network. Updating one is straightforward. Try these in order:

Check Windows Update first. Press the Windows key , type Windows Update , open it, then click Advanced options , then Optional updates . Driver updates often wait there. Install anything listed and restart.

Then try Device Manager. Press the Windows key , type Device Manager , and open it. Find the device Windows named, right-click it, choose Update driver , then Search automatically for drivers .

Then try the maker’s website. Search for the device name plus the word driver . Download only from the manufacturer’s own site — never from a search advert or a “driver updater” program.

Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates
Copy

What if there is no updated driver? This happens, usually with older hardware or a program the maker no longer supports. You have three choices, and none of them puts your PC at risk:

1. Leave Memory Integrity off and carry on. This is a perfectly reasonable outcome. Everything else Checkup set up still protects you. Memory Integrity is one layer among many.

2. Check again in a few months. Makers do release updates later. Repeat the four check steps above now and then.

3. If the program is one you no longer use, remove it. Press the Windows key , type Installed apps , find it, and uninstall it. Once its driver is gone, try turning Memory Integrity on again. Only do this for a program you are sure you do not need.

If you use antivirus other than Microsoft Defender , that is a common cause of this. If Windows reports driver problems after the restart, turn Memory Integrity back off using the same four steps, and try again once that program has been updated.

#### How to undo it

Follow the same four steps and set Memory integrity to Off , then restart. Nothing is deleted and none of your files are affected, either way.

#### What to expect after

You must restart. Until you do, nothing has changed.

You may notice two new entries in Task Manager. Memory Integrity is what creates vmmem and vmwp , which together use about 150–300 MB of memory. That is expected and it is doing its job. Leave them alone — do not try to end them.

Everything else should feel the same. On a typical home PC there is no difference in speed for day-to-day use.

Edge Password Saving

Setting 15 of 19

### Edge Password Saving

Edge offers to save your passwords so it can fill them in automatically. It is convenient, but it stores all your passwords in one place tied to your browser — if your PC is compromised, every saved password goes with it.

▶ Your decision

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews Edge’s password saving and autofill. It can turn that off with your permission — and only if you have told Checkup you already use a separate password manager.

Action taken: Checkup turned off Edge’s password saving offer with your approval. This does not delete any passwords already saved — it only stops Edge from offering to save new ones going forward.

#### Why you might want this off

A browser password manager is a convenient single point of failure. If someone gets into your Windows account — either by sitting down at your PC or by malware running on it — they can export every password Edge has saved in a few clicks. All your banking, email, and shopping accounts go at once.

A dedicated password manager like Bitwarden (free) or 1Password keeps your passwords in an encrypted vault that requires its own separate master password to open. Even if someone gets into your Windows account, they still cannot get into your password vault without that second password.

#### How to check it yourself

Open Microsoft Edge .

Click the three dots ( ⋯ ) in the top right, then click Settings .

Click Passwords in the left sidebar.

Confirm Offer to save passwords is set to Off .

#### How to turn it back on if you want it

Open Edge › Settings › Passwords.

Toggle Offer to save passwords to On .

Already have passwords saved in Edge? Turning off the offer to save does not delete them. To see or delete saved passwords, go to Edge › Settings › Passwords and scroll down to the list. You can export them from there before deleting if you want to move them to a dedicated password manager.

#### What to expect

Edge will no longer pop up asking if you want to save a password when you log into a website. Any passwords already saved in Edge continue to autofill as before until you delete them. No other feature of Edge is affected.

Recommended free alternative: Bitwarden. Bitwarden is a free, open-source password manager that works in Edge, Chrome, Firefox, and on your phone. It stores your passwords in an encrypted vault and fills them in automatically — with the added protection of a separate master password. Visit bitwarden.com to get started.

Home ›

Password Required on Wake

Setting 17 of 19

### Password Required on Wake

When your PC wakes from sleep, it should ask for your sign-in before showing your desktop. Without this, anyone who walks up to your sleeping laptop can use it immediately — no password required.

✎ You set this up

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews the sign-in requirement when your PC wakes from sleep. It can turn that on with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup reviews the setting and flags it if sign-in on wake is not required. This is a manual setup — the steps below show you exactly how to turn it on.

#### Why this matters

Sleep is not the same as off. When a laptop lid is closed or a PC goes to sleep, it looks off but all your open files, browser tabs, and accounts are still active in memory. If someone opens the lid and there is no sign-in prompt, they walk straight into your session — email, banking, everything.

This setting makes sure your PC asks for your PIN or password every time it wakes up. It takes two seconds and closes a gap that is easy to overlook.

#### How to set it up

Press the Windows key , type Sign-in options , and press Enter .

Under Require sign-in , click the dropdown.

Select When PC wakes from sleep .

Close Settings. The change takes effect immediately — no restart needed.

#### How to check if it is already on

Press Windows key , type Sign-in options , press Enter .

Under Require sign-in , check what the dropdown shows. It should say When PC wakes from sleep . If it says Never , follow the steps above to change it.

#### What to expect

The next time your PC wakes from sleep, it will show the lock screen and ask for your PIN, fingerprint, or password before continuing. This applies when you close the laptop lid, press the power button briefly, or the PC goes to sleep automatically after a period of inactivity.

Also check your sleep timer. If your PC never goes to sleep on its own, this setting has less effect. Open Settings > System > Power and make sure your PC is set to sleep after 10–15 minutes of inactivity. That way the lock kicks in automatically when you step away.

Defender Periodic Scanning

Setting 5 of 19

### Defender Periodic Scanning

If you use Malwarebytes as your main antivirus, Defender steps back and lets it run. Periodic Scanning keeps Defender running quiet monthly checks in the background as a second opinion — so you get two scanners for the price of none.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews Defender Periodic Scanning. This setting only appears when another antivirus program is active — if Defender is your primary antivirus, the option is hidden because Defender is already scanning continuously. Windows does not allow this one to be changed by a program, so Checkup shows you the exact steps instead.

Action taken: If periodic scanning was off and Malwarebytes was your primary antivirus, Checkup flagged it and offered to turn it on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

Two scanners catch more than one. Malwarebytes and Defender use different detection methods. Running both means a threat that slips past one may still be caught by the other. With Periodic Scanning on, Defender runs a quiet background check once a month without interfering with Malwarebytes at all.

If Defender is already your primary antivirus — with no Malwarebytes installed — this setting does not appear. Defender is already doing continuous scanning and Periodic Scanning is not needed.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key , type Windows Security , and press Enter .

Click Virus & threat protection .

Scroll down to Microsoft Defender Antivirus options . If you see this section, another antivirus is active and Periodic Scanning is available.

Click Microsoft Defender Antivirus options to expand it.

Confirm Periodic scanning is set to On . If it says Off, turn it on.

Do not see Microsoft Defender Antivirus options? That means Defender is your primary antivirus and is already scanning continuously. Periodic Scanning does not apply to you — this is normal and correct.

#### What to expect

With Periodic Scanning on, Defender runs a background scan roughly once a month. You will not notice it during normal use — it runs quietly when your PC is idle. If it finds something, it will alert you just like any Defender notification. It does not conflict with Malwarebytes or slow down your PC in any meaningful way.

Recommended scan schedule alongside Periodic Scanning: Run a Malwarebytes Custom Scan (with rootkit scanning checked) once a month, and a Malwarebytes Deep Scan quarterly. Periodic Scanning adds Defender’s monthly check on top of that, giving you the best coverage from both programs.

### Enhanced Phishing Protection

Windows watches for situations where you type your Windows password somewhere you shouldn’t — like a fake website or an unsecured document. When it sees this, it warns you before the damage is done.

✓ GatewayGuard Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews all three Enhanced Phishing Protection settings. It can turn them on with your permission, or show you the exact steps if Windows blocks the change.

Action taken: If any of the three settings were off, Checkup flagged them and offered to turn them on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

Phishing is one of the most reported online crimes against older adults. In 2025, people aged 60 and over filed more than 200,000 complaints with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, and phishing and spoofing were among the most reported. A fake website that looks like your bank, a pop-up asking you to sign in, an email link that takes you to a convincing copy of a real site — the goal is the same every time: get your password.

Source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, 2025 Internet Crime Report .

These three settings give Windows awareness of when your Windows password is being typed somewhere risky, and alert you before you accidentally hand it over.

Under Phishing protection , toggle each item that is off to On .

#### What to expect

No restart required. The protection is active immediately. You’ll only notice it if you type your Windows password somewhere it flags as risky — you’ll see a pop-up warning.

### Readable text

Home ›
Guide ›
Remote Desktop

Setting 10 of 19

### Remote Desktop

Remote Desktop lets someone connect to your PC over the internet and control it as if they were sitting in front of it. If you do not use this feature, leaving it on opens a door that does not need to be open.

✎ You set this up

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews the setting that allows inbound connections from other computers. On Windows 11 Pro , it can disable Remote Desktop with your permission. Windows 11 Home does not have this setting. Outbound connections to other devices are handled separately and are not affected.

Action taken: Checkup flagged Remote Desktop if it was on and asked for your approval to turn it off. If you use Remote Desktop intentionally — for example, to connect to your home PC from work — you can leave it on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

An open remote-access path is a security hole attackers actively look for. If your PC can be reached and controlled remotely, and someone guesses or steals your password, they are in. They can see your screen, open your files, and do anything you can do on your own machine — from anywhere in the world.

If your machine can be reached remotely and also has Remote Desktop or any other remote-access method enabled, this combination is a security hole attackers specifically scan for. Turning it off prevents this entirely. If you have never used Remote Desktop, you do not need it — and if you are not sure that you use it, you almost certainly do not.

#### How to turn it off

Press the Windows key , type Remote Desktop settings , and press Enter .

Click the toggle next to Remote Desktop to turn it Off .

Click Confirm when Windows asks if you are sure.

No restart required. Remote Desktop is off immediately.

Windows 11 Home users: nothing can connect in to your PC. This setting does not exist on your PC, and you do not need to do anything here. Remote Desktop is the Windows feature that lets another computer connect in to yours, and Windows 11 Home does not have it. There is no setting to leave on by mistake, and nothing sitting there waiting for a connection — not from a stranger, and not from Microsoft.

The one thing that can still let someone in is you. Separate helper programs — Quick Assist , which comes with Windows, and others such as TeamViewer — let someone see or control your screen, but only if you say yes at the time . They cannot start on their own and nobody can use them without your permission. That is what the scam call is for: someone claims to be from Microsoft and needs to connect to fix a problem. If you say yes, they are in — not because your PC is unprotected, but because you let them in. Microsoft will never call you. Hang up.

#### How to check if it is already off

Press Windows key , type Remote Desktop settings , press Enter .

The toggle should show Off . If it shows On, follow the steps above to turn it off.

#### What if I actually use Remote Desktop?

If you use Remote Desktop to connect to your home PC from another location, you can leave it on — but take these steps to reduce the risk:

Make sure your Windows account has a strong password — at least 12 characters with a mix of letters, numbers, and symbols.

In Remote Desktop settings, click Advanced settings and confirm Network Level Authentication is on. It should say On. If it does not, turn it on.

Under Remote Desktop users , confirm only your own account is listed. If you see any account you do not recognise, remove it by clicking it and selecting Remove.

Remote support scam warning: If anyone calls you unsolicited and asks you to turn on Remote Desktop or install remote-access software, hang up. Legitimate support staff from Microsoft, your bank, or your internet provider will never call you and ask for remote access to your PC.

#### Can you use Remote Desktop to connect out to another PC?

Yes. Windows 11 Home includes an app called Remote Desktop Connection that connects out to another computer — a work computer, for example. You may see it on your PC and wonder if it is a problem. It is not: it connects out, and it does not let anything connect in.

Our recommendation: if you do not use it, leave it off. If it is already off, leave it alone — there is nothing to turn off. If you use it for work, carry on. Either way, nothing can connect in to this PC, unless you let them. Never let them unless you started the contact yourself.

Do not install other remote-access programs unless you specifically need one and went looking for it yourself. Never install one because someone contacted you and asked you to.

### SmartScreen

SmartScreen checks files you download and websites you visit against a constantly updated list of known threats. It’s the warning that appears when you try to run something Microsoft doesn’t recognize — and the block that stops known-bad sites before they load.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews SmartScreen for apps, files, and browser content. It can turn it on with your permission.

Action taken: If any SmartScreen setting was off, Checkup flagged it and offered to turn it on. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

Malware usually arrives disguised as something normal — a free program, a PDF, a link in an email. It very often comes from a search result for a free tool. SmartScreen checks what you’re about to open or visit against Microsoft’s threat database before anything runs.

It has three separate layers: one for apps and files you download, one for websites you visit in Edge, and one that warns you when a site asks for your Microsoft account password. All three should be on.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key and type Windows Security , then press Enter .

Click App & browser control .

Click Reputation-based protection settings .

Confirm all of the following are set to On : Check apps and files , SmartScreen for Microsoft Edge , Potentially unwanted app blocking , and SmartScreen for Microsoft Store apps .

Scroll down to Phishing protection . Confirm all three sub-options are On : Warn me about malicious apps and sites , Warn me about password reuse , and Warn me about unsafe password storage .

#### How to change it yourself

Open Windows Security > App & browser control > Reputation-based protection settings .

Toggle any items that are off to On .

No restart required.

#### What to expect

SmartScreen works in the background. You’ll only see it if you try to download or run something it doesn’t recognize — in which case it shows a warning screen. You can still choose to run the file if you trust it; SmartScreen just makes sure you saw the warning first.

SmartScreen shows a warning on a file I downloaded. Read the warning carefully. If you downloaded the file from a well-known source (the software company’s own website, for example) and you were expecting it, you can choose to run it anyway. If you’re not sure, don’t run it.

- **Measured:** full name 1 in body / 0 in meta - "Checkup" 7 - "whether" 0 - "switch" 0 verb / 0 word - permission named 4

### Readable text

Home ›
Guide ›
Wake on LAN

Setting 19 of 19

### Wake on LAN (explained fully below)

This setting lets another computer turn your PC on from across your home network, while your PC is asleep. It was built for offices. Almost no home user needs it, and leaving it on keeps a door open that nobody is watching.

▶ Your decision — GatewayGuard asked before changing it

#### What GatewayGuard Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your PC’s Wake on LAN setting. Some PCs cannot do it at all, and Checkup simply moves past those. Where it can be changed, Checkup asks your permission first.

Action taken: If it was turned on, Checkup explained what it does and asked for your permission to turn it off. Nothing was changed unless you said yes.

#### Why this matters

Wake on LAN and Remote Desktop are the two “let someone in from outside” features on a home PC. We strongly recommend both be off. (LAN is just a name for your home network — the wired and wireless connections between the machines in your house.)

This setting exists so an office can turn on hundreds of computers overnight to install updates. That is a real need — in an office. At home, it means your PC can be woken by something other than you, and a PC that can be woken is a PC that can be reached when you are not sitting in front of it.

On its own, this does not let anyone into your PC. It is the combination that matters: a machine that can be turned on remotely, plus any other way in, is worth far more to an attacker than either one alone. Turning it off costs you nothing if you never used it — and if you are reading this page, you almost certainly never used it.

#### The phone call you should expect one day

##### If anyone ever phones you and asks you to turn remote access on — hang up.

The same goes for anyone who asks you to install a program so they can “connect to your computer and fix it.” It does not matter if they say they are from Microsoft, from your bank, from your internet provider, or from a company whose name you recognise.

Older adults lose money to this scam far more often than younger adults do. That is the Federal Trade Commission’s finding, and it reports that the caller often claims to be from Microsoft or Apple. Microsoft does not phone people. Your bank does not need to control your PC. A real company will never call you out of the blue and ask for remote access.

Hang up. If you are worried it might have been genuine, look up the company’s real number yourself — on your bank card, on a statement, on their official website — and call them back on that number. Never a number the caller gave you.

#### How to check it, and turn it off

Press the Windows key , type Device Manager , and open it.

Click the arrow next to Network adapters to open the list. (A network adapter is the part of your PC that connects it to the internet. Many PCs have two — one for Wi-Fi, one for the cable socket.)

Right-click the first one and choose Properties .

Click the Power Management tab. If there is no tab with that name, this one cannot wake your PC and there is nothing to change — close it and go to the next one.

Find Allow this device to wake the computer . The box should be empty. If there is a tick in it, click it to remove the tick , then click OK .

Repeat for your other network adapter. Both need doing — turning off one and not the other leaves the door open.

No restart is needed. The change works straight away. Here is the path if you would rather paste it than type it:

Device Manager > Network adapters > Properties > Power Management
Copy

#### Do I need to change anything in the startup screen settings?

No. The Windows setting above is the one that matters, and it is enough.

You may read elsewhere that this feature also has a setting in the settings screen that appears before Windows starts. That is true on some PCs, but it does not override what you just did — with the Windows box unticked, your PC will not be woken from the network. You do not need to go near those settings, and we do not recommend it. They differ on every make of PC and a wrong change there is much harder to undo.

#### If you actually use this feature

Some people do use it on purpose — for example, turning on a PC in another room from a phone app so it is ready when they get there. If that is you, leave it on. This is a recommendation, not a requirement, which is why Checkup asked instead of just changing it.

If you keep it on, make it safer. In the same Power Management tab, look for Only allow a magic packet to wake the computer and put a tick in that box. A magic packet is a specific “wake up” message meant only for your PC. With that ticked, ordinary network chatter can no longer wake it — only a deliberate signal will.

A note on Fast Startup. GatewayGuard also turns off Fast Startup (Setting 18), for reasons explained on that page . The two settings interact on some PCs. If you keep Wake on LAN on and it stops working reliably, the two are worth looking at together.

#### How to undo it

Go back to the same place — Device Manager , Network adapters , right-click the adapter, Properties , Power Management — and put the tick back in Allow this device to wake the computer . Nothing is lost by turning it off and back on.

Device Manager > Network adapters > Properties > Power Management
Copy

#### What to expect after

Your PC still wakes up normally. Opening the lid, pressing the power button, moving the mouse, or pressing a key all work exactly as before. The one thing that stops is another machine waking it — which is the point.

Source: Federal Trade Commission, Protecting Older Consumers 2024–2025 .

Your scheduled reminders still run. The monthly and quarterly scan reminders Checkup set up are scheduled inside Windows and do not depend on this setting.

### Windows Widgets

Windows Widgets is the news, weather, and sports panel that appears on your taskbar. It sends information about what you read and click back to Microsoft. Turning it off removes the panel and stops that data sharing.

▶ Your decision

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews Windows Widgets on your taskbar. It can turn it off with your permission.

Action taken: Checkup turned off Windows Widgets with your approval. If you use and enjoy the Widgets panel, you can turn it back on at any time — the steps are below.

#### Why you might want this off

Widgets sends your reading and browsing habits back to Microsoft. The panel is powered by Microsoft Start, and it tracks which stories you read, how long you spend on them, and what you click on — to serve you more personalized content. If you do not want Microsoft collecting that information, turning Widgets off is the clean solution.

There is also a background process involved. Widgets uses the Edge browser engine (WebView2) to run even when you are not looking at it. Turning it off frees up that memory and removes a process that was running without you asking for it.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key , type Taskbar settings , and press Enter .

Look for Widgets in the list. If the toggle is Off , Widgets is disabled.

#### How to turn it back on if you want it

Press the Windows key , type Taskbar settings , and press Enter .

Toggle Widgets to On .

The Widgets button reappears on your taskbar immediately. No restart needed.

#### What to expect

With Widgets off, the weather and news icon disappears from your taskbar. Your PC will use slightly less memory in the background. Everything else on your PC works exactly the same. If you want news or weather, your browser works just as well for that.

This is more than a taste. The panel builds a record of what you read and click, and it keeps a background process running when you are not looking at it. Anything still running is still working. Checkup turns it off with your permission, and you can turn it back on whenever you like.

### Windows Hello

Windows Hello lets you sign in with a PIN, fingerprint, or face instead of a password. It is faster, more convenient, and harder for someone else to use — a PIN only works on your specific PC, unlike a password that works anywhere.

✎ You set this up

#### What Checkup found and did

Found: Checkup reviews your Windows Hello setup — a PIN, fingerprint, or face sign-in. Windows requires you to set this up yourself, so Checkup shows you the steps rather than doing it for you.

Action taken: Checkup reviews your Windows Hello setup and flags it if no sign-in method is configured. This is a manual setup — Checkup cannot set up your PIN or fingerprint for you because Windows requires you to confirm your identity as part of the process.

#### Why this matters

A PIN is safer than a password for signing into Windows. That sounds backwards, but here is why it is true: your password works on any device, anywhere — if someone learns it, they can use it from the other side of the world. A Windows Hello PIN only works on your specific PC. It never leaves your device and is never sent over the internet. If someone learns your PIN, they still cannot use it without physical access to your computer.

Fingerprint and face sign-in go one step further — only you can use them. They are also faster than typing a password every time you sit down.

#### How to set it up

Press the Windows key , type Sign-in options , and press Enter .

You will see options for Windows Hello PIN , Fingerprint recognition , and Facial recognition . At minimum, set up a PIN — it is available on every PC.

Click Windows Hello PIN , then click Add .

Windows will ask you to verify your Microsoft account password first. Enter it and click OK .

Choose a PIN of at least 6 digits. Avoid obvious patterns like 123456 or your birth year. Click OK .

Done. Next time you sign in, Windows will show a PIN prompt instead of a password prompt.

Also set up fingerprint or face if your PC supports it. Check under Fingerprint recognition or Facial recognition in the same Sign-in options screen. If your PC has a fingerprint reader or front camera with infrared support, these options will be available. If they are grayed out, your PC hardware does not support them — the PIN is sufficient.

#### How to check if it is already set up

Press Windows key , type Sign-in options , press Enter .

If Windows Hello PIN shows a Change button, a PIN is already set up. If it shows Add , it is not set up yet.

#### What to expect

Once set up, Windows will use your PIN or biometric by default at the sign-in screen. You can still sign in with your password if needed by clicking Sign-in options on the lock screen. Your PIN and fingerprint data never leave your PC — they are stored in a secure chip on your device, not in Microsoft’s servers.

Forgot your PIN? On the sign-in screen, click I forgot my PIN . Windows will verify your Microsoft account password and let you set a new one. You will not lose any files or settings.

Windows Update

Setting 1 of 19

### Windows Update

Keeps your PC current with the latest security fixes from Microsoft. Attackers routinely target security holes that Microsoft has already fixed. The fix only protects you once it is installed.

✓ Checkup can do this for you

#### What Checkup found and did

Found:
Checkup reviews Windows Update and its automatic update settings, including updates for other Microsoft products. It can turn automatic updates back on with your permission.

Action taken:
If Windows Update was disabled or set to manual-only, Checkup flagged it and walked you through re-enabling it. No changes are made without your approval.

#### Why this matters

Hackers look for PCs that haven’t been updated. When Microsoft finds a security hole in Windows, they release a patch. The moment that patch is public, attackers know exactly what the hole is — and start scanning for PCs that haven’t installed the fix yet.

Keeping Windows Update on is simple, costs you nothing, and protects you automatically in the background.

#### How to check it yourself

Press the Windows key on your keyboard (the key with the Windows logo), then type Windows Update and press Enter .

The Windows Update page opens. Click Check for updates . Windows will look for anything new and download it automatically.

Scroll down and click Advanced options . Make sure these three toggles are turned On :

• Receive updates for other Microsoft products — covers Office, Edge, and other Microsoft software

• Download updates over metered connections — optional, but recommended if you’re on a fast home connection

• Notify me when a restart is required to finish updating — so Windows doesn’t restart at a bad time

Go back to the main Windows Update page. If updates are listed, let them download and install. Click Restart now if prompted — the restart is what completes the installation.

What version of Windows 11 are you on? To check: on the Windows Update page, scroll down and look for Windows 11, version 24H2 (or higher). If you see an older version, click Check for updates and let it install the latest. Windows 10 reaches its end of support on October 14, 2025 — if your PC still runs Windows 10, it will no longer receive security updates after that date.

#### How to turn it back on if it’s off

Press Windows + R on your keyboard. A small “Run” box appears.

Type services.msc and press Enter . A list of Windows services opens.

Scroll down to find Windows Update . Right-click it and choose Properties .

Under Startup type , change the setting from Disabled or Manual to Automatic . Click Apply , then OK .

Right-click Windows Update again and choose Start . Then go back to Settings › Windows Update and click Check for updates .

#### What to expect after updating

Updates usually install quietly in the background. Some require a restart to take effect — Windows will tell you when. The restart usually takes 5–10 minutes. Your files and settings are not affected. After the restart, Windows is protected against the latest known security threats.

Updates feel slow? That’s normal the first time if your PC has been off for a while. It’s downloading several months of patches at once. After that, updates are small and fast.
